model: Doctor-founded telehealth brand that sells compounded topical finasteride, dutasteride and finasteride-plus-minoxidil in its patented SiloxysSystem gel (plus oral options and hair-care cosmetics), prescribed after an online questionnaire and photo review, with a second channel through partner hair clinics.

access.accountWall: After the eligibility gate. Men answer 4 questions (country, state or province, date of birth, biological sex), women 5 (plus pregnancy / conception / breastfeeding / fertility), then see "Congrats! You are eligible." and must create an account (legal first and last name, email, password, consent tick-box). The whole medical history, treatment preference, plan choice, photos and ID sit behind that account. Nothing is recommended before the wall.
blockers: Medical-history question wording is only served after sign-in: /en-US/hair-treatment-rx/mens/new and /womens/new redirect anonymous visitors to /en-US/login, and the JS chunk for those routes is not referenced by any public page.
Web search was unavailable (shared search budget used up), so third-party reviews, press and regulator listings were not checked.
Four help-centre articles linked from the help index return 404 (ineligible conditions; which topical is right for me; treatments for men; treatments for women).
access.coverageNote: Stage 1 (map). Walked live: the full anonymous eligibility flow for the baseline man and woman up to the account form, one stop screen (pregnancy = Yes), and the 3-question marketing quiz. Read from publicly served code: the whole eligibility schema with every branch and stop reason, the country and region lists, the product and variant enums, the field keys and step groups of the signed-in medical history (keys only, not wording), feature flags. Read from public pages: the Shopify product feed (all 64 products with prices and sex-eligibility tags), seven prescription product pages with safety information, the how-it-works page, help-centre articles and policies. Not tested: anything after the account wall, Canadian (en-CA) prices and wording, one-change experiments.

flows.stagesSummary: Welcome screen → 4 anonymous eligibility questions for men (country, state or province, date of birth, biological sex), 5 for women (plus pregnancy / conception / breastfeeding / fertility) → "Congrats! recommendations.profile: Woman, 38, California, not pregnant: real consultation
recommendations.note: Same: eligible, then account wall, no product shown.

engineSummary: XYON's public engine is only a gate, not a recommender. Four or five anonymous questions check where you live, that you are 18 or over, your biological sex and, for women, pregnancy, conception, breastfeeding or fertility treatment. Pass and you must create an account; fail and you are asked for an email for updates (or, in 28 European countries, sent to a partner). The real decision happens after sign-in: a medical history (hair-loss history, earlier treatments and why they were stopped, mental health, cancer, sexual and urinary history, general conditions, blood pressure, kidney, medicines, allergies, pregnancy in the household), then the patient states a treatment preference and an application method (Topical, Topical low dose, Oral, or no preference), picks a plan, uploads scalp photos and photo ID, and a doctor chooses the medicine. Sex limits the product set through tags on the checkout products: finasteride-only gel and finasteride tablets are for men, spironolactone is for women, the rest are for both. The "personalised" quiz on the marketing site always recommends the same gel.
strengths: A clear technical story: one patented gel base (SiloxysSystem, US patent 11,786,466) with published absorption claims ("92% less absorbed into the blood than pills") and doctor founders.
Honest, prominent compounded-medicine and safety notices on every prescription page.
Very short eligibility gate (4 to 5 taps) before the account wall.
Serves women with the same flow, with a hard pregnancy and fertility stop before any data is collected.
A second route to market through 100+ partner hair-restoration clinics (ClinicConnect).
Simple plan logic: subscription includes the consultation; one-time orders pay $20.
weaknesses: No recommendation or price is shown before sign-up: the visitor must give a legal name, email and password to learn anything personal.
The marketing quiz is not real: every answer leads to the same product.
Premium prices ($109 to $139 a month for the gels) against cheaper compounded sprays elsewhere.
The finasteride and minoxidil solution's strengths are not published on its page.
Help centre has dead links for the articles on who is ineligible and which treatment suits whom.
Review time is stated inconsistently (24–48 hours on product pages, 3–5 business days on the how-it-works page).
Photo ID step adds friction (they are testing its removal on half of US visitors).
opportunities: Show a genuine, answer-driven recommendation with price before asking for an account.
Publish plain eligibility rules (conditions and medicines that rule each treatment out) instead of leaving them to the doctor review.
Offer a lower-priced controlled-release topical, or publish strengths and absorption data for every formula.
Give women a tailored path (menopause, contraception, PCOS questions) rather than one shared flow with a single pregnancy gate.

limitations: The medical-history questions are known only as field keys from public code. Their wording, options, order and branch conditions were not seen, because they are served only after an account is created.
Some field keys in the shared enum (nitroglycerin, recreational drugs, serious cardiac episode) may belong to the sexual-health flow, not the hair flow.
What the doctor prescribes for a given patient cannot be observed. Sex-based product limits are read from Shopify product tags, not from a live result.
US prices only (en-US). Canadian prices and the en-CA flow were not checked.
The strengths of the finasteride and minoxidil solution, and the vitamin D dose in the compounded minoxidil tablet, are not published on the pages read.
No web search was possible in this session, so no third-party reviews, press or regulator records were used.
Only the pregnancy stop screen was seen live; the age, region and European-partner screens are from the code.
